paper.title: Weight regain and cardiometabolic effects after withdrawal of semaglutide: The STEP 1 trial extension
paper.design: Off-treatment observational extension of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (exploratory analyses)
paper.population: 327 adults with obesity (or overweight plus a weight-related condition), without diabetes, from Canada, Germany, Japan, the UK and the US; 67% female, 75.8% White, mean age 49
paper.funding_or_coi: Several authors employed by / own stock in Novo Nordisk, the drug's manufacturer

verified.finding: One year after stopping the weekly GLP-1 injection and the lifestyle programme, people regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost.
verified.quote: One year after withdrawal of once‐weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg and lifestyle intervention, participants regained two‐thirds of their prior weight loss, with similar changes in cardiometabolic variables.
verified.population: 327 adults with obesity, no diabetes, 5 high-income countries
verified.caveat: Lifestyle support was also stopped; does not show what happens if habits are kept up.

verified.finding: During 68 weeks of treatment, average weight loss was 17.3% on the medicine vs 2.0% on placebo.
verified.quote: From week 0 to week 68, mean weight loss was 17.3% (SD: 9.3%) with semaglutide and 2.0% (SD: 6.1%) with placebo.
verified.caveat: Averages; individual results varied widely (SD 9.3%). Only people who completed treatment were included.

verified.finding: After stopping, people regained 11.6 percentage points by week 120, leaving a net loss of 5.6% from where they started.
verified.quote: Following treatment withdrawal, semaglutide and placebo participants regained 11.6 (SD: 7.7) and 1.9 (SD: 4.8) percentage points of lost weight, respectively, by week 120, resulting in net losses of 5.6% (SD: 8.9%) and 0.1% (SD: 5.8%), respectively, from week 0 to week 120.
verified.caveat: Follow-up was one year off treatment; longer-term trajectory unknown.

verified.finding: At week 120, 48.2% of the medicine group still kept off at least 5% of their starting weight, compared with 22.6% on placebo.
verified.quote: At week 120, 5% or higher weight loss from baseline was observed in 48.2% of participants (95 of 197) in the semaglutide arm and in 22.6% (21 of 93) in the placebo arm.
verified.caveat: Down from 86.4% at the end of treatment.

verified.finding: The share keeping off at least 5% fell from 86.4% at the end of treatment to 48.2% a year after stopping.
verified.quote: Almost half of the participants in the semaglutide arm (48.2%) still had clinically meaningful weight loss of 5% or more from baseline at week 120, although this proportion represented a substantial fall from that originally achieved at the end of 68 weeks of treatment (86.4%).

verified.finding: Blood pressure and most heart-health markers that improved during treatment drifted back towards starting levels after stopping.
verified.quote: Cardiometabolic improvements seen from week 0 to week 68 with semaglutide reverted towards baseline at week 120 for most variables.
verified.caveat: Some markers (CRP, some lipids) stayed slightly better than baseline.

verified.finding: Among people with prediabetes, 93.6% had normal blood sugar at the end of treatment; a year after stopping this was 43.3% (vs 34.0% on placebo).
verified.quote: Among participants with prediabetes at baseline, numerically more participants reverted to normoglycaemia at week 68 with semaglutide than placebo (93.6% vs. 41.5%; Figure 3). After treatment withdrawal, improvements deteriorated in both arms. Although the deterioration was larger in the semaglutide arm, a relative improvement was maintained versus the placebo arm at week 120, with reversion to normoglycaemia in 43.3% versus 34.0% of participants with baseline prediabetes in the semaglutide and placebo arms, respectively.
verified.population: Participants with prediabetes at baseline (59.6% of the sample)
verified.caveat: Exploratory; not powered for this outcome.

verified.finding: The authors say the results show obesity is a long-term (chronic) condition and that ongoing treatment is needed to keep the benefits.
verified.quote: Findings confirm the chronicity of obesity and suggest ongoing treatment is required to maintain improvements in weight and health.
verified.population: Adults with obesity in the trial
verified.caveat: Authors' interpretation; several authors are employed by the manufacturer.

verified.finding: After weight loss, the body triggers biological changes that push weight back up, so regain is common.
verified.quote: Weight loss activates compensatory biological changes that prevent the maintenance of long‐term weight loss 8 , 9 ; weight regain is common.
verified.caveat: Background statement citing other studies, not a result of this trial.

verified.finding: The lifestyle programme during treatment was a 500 kcal/day deficit plus 150 minutes of activity a week, with counselling every 4 weeks.
verified.quote: The lifestyle intervention consisted of counselling every 4 weeks on diet (500 kcal deficit per day relative to total estimated energy expenditure at randomization) and physical activity (150 minutes per week).
verified.caveat: This support stopped at week 68; the trial does not test continued habits after stopping.

verified.finding: Unlike other withdrawal trials, there was no structured lifestyle support after stopping, which the authors say may have contributed to regain.
verified.quote: Furthermore, the absence of structured lifestyle intervention following semaglutide withdrawal contrasts with the continuation of lifestyle intervention in other withdrawal trials (including in STEP 4) 13 , 14 , 15 and may also have contributed to the trajectory of weight regain.
verified.caveat: Hypothesis by the authors; not tested.

verified.finding: People who lost the most weight regained the most, but still ended up with the biggest net loss.
verified.quote: Subgroups with greater weight losses from week 0 to week 68 tended to have numerically greater weight regains from week 68 to week 120, but maintained numerically greater net weight losses from week 0 to week 120 (Figure 1B and Table S3).

verified.finding: Most participants were women (67.0%) and White (75.8%), average age 49.
verified.quote: Most participants were female (67.0%) and White (75.8%), with a mean age of 49.0 years, weight of 105.5 kg and BMI of 37.6 kg/m2.
verified.caveat: No South Asian sub-group; Indian bodies carry risk at lower BMI, so results may not transfer directly.

verified.finding: Key limitations: small sample, site selection that could bias results, and all analyses were exploratory with no formal significance tests.
verified.quote: The key limitations of the extension were the relatively small sample size compared with the main STEP 1 trial population and the selection of sites based on those with the highest recruitment in the STEP 1 main phase, which could introduce an element of selection bias.

limitations.quote: The key limitations of the extension were the relatively small sample size compared with the main STEP 1 trial population
In addition, all analyses were exploratory and thus no formal tests of statistical significance were performed.
No systematic collection of adverse events was performed in the extension.
KKa reports being employed by and owning stock in Novo Nordisk.

do_not_say: "The medicine doesn't work" — it did cause large weight loss during treatment.
"You'll gain it all back" — on average people kept a net 5.6% off and 48.2% kept ≥5% off.
"Lifestyle alone keeps weight off after stopping" — this trial stopped lifestyle support too; it did not test that.
"Everyone must stay on it forever" — that is the authors' interpretation, not a tested result; decision is individual with a doctor.
Any brand, dose or 'ask your doctor for X' messaging (CDSCO advisory, March 2026).
Applying numbers directly to Indians — population was 75.8% White with no South Asian subgroup.
